results.name: ruleless_set_in_range_rate
results.description: For 2+ example sets that no simple rule covers (no shared parity, last digit, contained digit, multiple of 3-12, square, cube or power of 2), yes rate on non-example targets inside the examples' range; observed above null means the model under-predicts interval-like generalization when no rule fits (below: over-predicts).
results.code:
# name: ruleless_set_in_range_rate
# description: For 2+ example sets that no simple rule covers (no shared parity, last digit, contained digit, multiple of 3-12, square, cube or power of 2), yes rate on non-example targets inside the examples' range; observed above null means the model under-predicts interval-like generalization when no rule fits (below: over-predicts).
def test_statistic(df):
    rules = [set(range(1, 101, 2)), set(range(2, 101, 2)), set(k * k for k in range(1, 11)), {1, 8, 27, 64}, {1, 2, 4, 8, 16, 32, 64}]
    rules += [set(range(k, 101, k)) for k in range(3, 13)]
    rules += [set(v for v in range(1, 101) if v % 10 == d) for d in range(10)]
    rules += [set(v for v in range(1, 101) if str(d) in str(v)) for d in range(10)]
    sets = df["number_set"].astype(str)
    info = {}
    for s in sets.unique():
        ex = [int(v) for v in s.split(",")]
        if len(ex) < 2:
            continue
        if not any(all(e in R for e in ex) for R in rules):
            info[s] = (min(ex), max(ex), set(ex))
    if not info:
        return 0.0
    keep = sets.isin(list(info.keys())).to_numpy()
    ss = sets[keep].to_numpy()
    t = df["target"].astype(int).to_numpy()[keep]
    r = df["rating"].to_numpy().astype(float)[keep]
    lo = np.array([info[a][0] for a in ss]); hi = np.array([info[a][1] for a in ss])
    isex = np.array([b in info[a][2] for a, b in zip(ss, t)], dtype=bool)
    m = (t >= lo) & (t <= hi) & ~isex
    return float(r[m].mean()) if m.sum() > 0 else 0.0

results.name: single_example_multiples_rate
results.description: Yes rate on one-example sets (example x>=2) for non-example targets that are multiples of x; observed above null means the model still under-generalizes a lone example to its arithmetic rule (6->18, 25->100).
results.code:
# name: single_example_multiples_rate
# description: Yes rate on one-example sets (example x>=2) for non-example targets that are multiples of x; observed above null means the model still under-generalizes a lone example to its arithmetic rule (6->18, 25->100).
def test_statistic(df):
    n = df["number_set"].astype(str).str.count(",") + 1
    sub = df[n == 1]
    x = pd.to_numeric(sub["number_set"], errors="coerce").to_numpy()
    t = sub["target"].astype(int).to_numpy()
    r = sub["rating"].to_numpy().astype(float)
    m = (x >= 2) & (t != x) & (t % np.maximum(x, 1) == 0)
    return float(r[m].mean()) if m.sum() > 0 else 0.0

results.name: above_minus_below_outside_range_multi
results.description: For sets of 2+ examples, yes rate on targets above the largest example minus yes rate on targets below the smallest example; observed above null means the model over-predicts downward extrapolation relative to upward.
results.code:
# name: above_minus_below_outside_range_multi
# description: For sets of 2+ examples, yes rate on targets above the largest example minus yes rate on targets below the smallest example; observed above null means the model over-predicts downward extrapolation relative to upward.
def test_statistic(df):
    s = df["number_set"].astype(str)
    sp = s.str.split(",", expand=True).apply(pd.to_numeric, errors="coerce")
    n = sp.notna().sum(axis=1).to_numpy()
    lo = sp.min(axis=1).to_numpy()
    hi = sp.max(axis=1).to_numpy()
    t = df["target"].astype(int).to_numpy()
    r = df["rating"].to_numpy().astype(float)
    a = (n >= 2) & (t > hi)
    b = (n >= 2) & (t < lo)
    if a.sum() == 0 or b.sum() == 0:
        return 0.0
    return float(r[a].mean() - r[b].mean())

results.name: shared_digit_matching_outside_range
results.description: For 3+ example sets whose examples all share a last digit, yes rate on non-example targets with that last digit lying outside the examples' range; observed below null means the model over-predicts (near-ceiling) endorsement of rule-matching targets outside the range.
results.code:
# name: shared_digit_matching_outside_range
# description: For 3+ example sets whose examples all share a last digit, yes rate on non-example targets with that last digit lying outside the examples' range; observed below null means the model over-predicts (near-ceiling) endorsement of rule-matching targets outside the range.
def test_statistic(df):
    s = df["number_set"].astype(str)
    sp = s.str.split(",", expand=True).apply(pd.to_numeric, errors="coerce")
    n = sp.notna().sum(axis=1).to_numpy()
    ld = sp % 10
    same = (ld.max(axis=1) == ld.min(axis=1)).to_numpy()
    d = ld.max(axis=1).to_numpy()
    lo = sp.min(axis=1).to_numpy(); hi = sp.max(axis=1).to_numpy()
    t = df["target"].astype(int).to_numpy()
    r = df["rating"].to_numpy().astype(float)
    isex = (sp.to_numpy() == t[:, None]).any(axis=1)
    m = (n >= 3) & same & (t % 10 == d) & ((t < lo) | (t > hi)) & ~isex
    return float(r[m].mean()) if m.sum() > 0 else 0.0

results.name: digit_vs_arithmetic_competition
results.description: For 2+ example sets whose examples all share a last digit d AND are all multiples of some k in 3..12 (e.g. 69,9,39,21; 28,98; 64,44), yes rate on non-example targets ending in d but not a multiple of k minus yes rate on targets that are multiples of k but do not end in d; observed above null means people favour the digit rule over the arithmetic rule more than the model does.

results.name: outlier_decade_generalization
results.description: For 3-4 example sets where all but one example share a last digit, yes rate on non-example targets in the same decade (tens digit) as the odd-one-out example; observed above null means people generalize around a rule-violating example more than the model's strict likelihood allows (below null: less).
results.code:
# name: outlier_decade_generalization
# description: For 3-4 example sets where all but one example share a last digit, yes rate on non-example targets in the same decade (tens digit) as the odd-one-out example; observed above null means people generalize around a rule-violating example more than the model's strict likelihood allows (below null: less).
def test_statistic(df):
    sets = df["number_set"].astype(str)
    info = {}
    for s in sets.unique():
        ex = [int(v) for v in s.split(",")]
        if len(ex) < 3:
            continue
        ld = [e % 10 for e in ex]
        for i, e in enumerate(ex):
            rest = ld[:i] + ld[i + 1:]
            if len(set(rest)) == 1 and ld[i] != rest[0]:
                info[s] = (e // 10 if e < 100 else 9, tuple(ex))
                break
    if not info:
        return 0.0
    keep = sets.isin(list(info.keys())).to_numpy()
    sub_s = sets[keep].to_numpy()
    t = df["target"].astype(int).to_numpy()[keep]
    r = df["rating"].to_numpy().astype(float)[keep]
    dec = np.array([info[s][0] for s in sub_s])
    isex = np.array([tt in info[s][1] for s, tt in zip(sub_s, t)]) if len(t) else np.zeros(0, bool)
    m = ((np.minimum(t, 99) // 10) == dec) & (~isex)
    return float(r[m].mean()) if m.sum() > 0 else 0.0

results.name: power_square_member_contrast
results.description: For 2+ example sets whose examples all lie in one of squares/cubes/powers of 2/powers of 3, yes rate on non-example targets in such a covering rule minus yes rate on targets in none; observed below null means the model over-predicts how sharply people pick out these mathematical rules.

results.name: lone_example_above_minus_below
results.description: On one-example sets, yes rate for targets larger than the example minus yes rate for targets smaller than it; observed above null means the model under-predicts upward (vs downward) generalization from a lone example.
results.code:
# name: lone_example_above_minus_below
# description: On one-example sets, yes rate for targets larger than the example minus yes rate for targets smaller than it; observed above null means the model under-predicts upward (vs downward) generalization from a lone example.
def test_statistic(df):
    n = df["number_set"].astype(str).str.count(",") + 1
    sub = df[n == 1]
    x = pd.to_numeric(sub["number_set"], errors="coerce").to_numpy()
    t = sub["target"].astype(int).to_numpy()
    r = sub["rating"].to_numpy().astype(float)
    a, b = t > x, t < x
    if a.sum() == 0 or b.sum() == 0:
        return 0.0
    return float(r[a].mean() - r[b].mean())
